title: The Accountability Gap
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Most leadership problems are not personality problems but accountability problems rooted in the leader's unwillingness to enforce standards due to discomfort-avoidance. Mulder shares her own failure to enforce expectations with talented team members, which cascaded through her organization, creating a culture that mirrored her avoidance. She argues that accountability is not aggression or harshness but clarity, alignment, and truth-telling about what is actually required to reach goals. When leaders avoid accountability to be perceived as kind, they are actually being unclear, and unclear leadership is expensive in trust, time, money, and respect. True accountability provides stability and tells the team exactly where they stand and what is expected.
points: Leaders often avoid accountability because they fear disappointing admired team members or being perceived as difficult, but this avoidance cascades as the team mirrors the leader's culture of lowered standards.
Accountability is not punishment; it is clarity, alignment, and stability, communicating to the team: This is where we're going. This is what it takes. And I believe you can do it.
People don't lose trust when you enforce a standard; they lose trust when you waffle, move the bar based on mood or fear, or tolerate different behavior from different people.
When accountability finally becomes the norm, clarity replaces chaos, ownership replaces excuses, and progress replaces drama, while those who resist the standard self-select out.
The question every leader should ask themselves is: Where am I avoiding accountability because I don't want to feel the friction? That answer reveals exactly where their next level is.
quotes: We say we want ownership. But what we really mean is: I want everyone else to take ownership.
Most leadership problems aren't personality problems. They're accountability problems.
When the leader avoids accountability, the team avoids accountability. When the leader softens the standard, the team softens the effort.
Avoiding accountability doesn't make you kind. It makes you unclear. And unclear leadership is expensive.
Accountability is not punishment. Accountability is stability. It tells the team: This is where we're going. This is what it takes. And I believe you can do it.

There's a freedom that comes when you stop avoiding accountability. A confidence. A groundedness. A sense of knowing you can handle whatever truth needs to be spoken.” Archived from Summer Mulder Substack on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
